paragraphs.text: Output house rules for every DeepSeek Harness agent: no check-mark or cross glyphs in replies or wri

orkspace and subagent obeys without a single preset edit.
# Oishikunaare-Moe-Moe-Kyun
> Chinese documentation: README.zh-CN.md
### What is verified where

An entry that has never met the thing it is written for is not the same as one that has, and the
dif
ference is worth stating instead of implying. This table is the honest version.
| entry | how it is verified |
| DSH plugin | In production on the machine this was written on: mounted in a live profile, and its

rules and self-check are visible in real sessions |
| CLI `mmk` | Used on that machine for real work
- auditing a session, answering whether a line would be refused - and exercised by `test/portable.m

js` |
| MCP server | The protocol is checked locally: a handshake, `tools/list`, every tool called,

`resources/read`. The client half depends on the client |
| Claude Code hook | **Documented contract
plus recorded fixtures only** (`npm run test:adapters`); never run against a live Claude Code, beca
use none is installed here. The contract has moved between releases, so treat this one as a candidat

e rather than a supported entry |
| rules files (`mmk wire ...-md`) | The block is generated from th
e same resolved rules the plugin serves, so the text is verified; whether a given program reads that
file is its own documentation |

When a harness that is not on this machine does become available, the way to close the gap is one
re
corded payload: save the stdin JSON a hook actually receives as `adapters/fixtures/<harness>/<case>.

json`
and `npm run test:adapters` replays it. That is what the fixture directory is for, and it is w

hy adding
an adapter is cheap once someone can run the client - and why writing five of them from me

er is cheap once someone can run the client - and why writing five of them from memory would not
be.
The DSH plugin row is worth explaining, because it is the anti-drift argument: a profile-level plugi

n is
mounted once by the roster, so the section it registers reaches every agent that joins that sta

nding
scope - every preset, every workspace, every new conversation, and subagents too. That is why

it is done
there rather than in fifteen preset files: a preset is a copy, and a copy is a thing that

drifts. The
other entries exist because the same rules are worth having where no such roster exists

drifts. The
other entries exist because the same rules are worth having where no such roster exists.
Four rules ship today.
[该节后续省略]
### What the review of the shipped material found

Checked on 2026-10-14 across `rules/voices/*.json` (18 marker sets, drawn from Moegirlpedia's
kuchig

use entry since they were added), `rules/kaomoji.json` and the examples inside the rule prose: no
hi
t for the jirai-kei family, for menhera / yandere vocabulary, for danmei or fandom-for-BL vocabulary

,
for the grotesque register named above, or for the practices the hygiene preference names. The onl

y
textual matches a keyword scan returns are the ordinary English word "small" and the identifier
`p

eerDependenciesMeta` - neither is a topic. The voice tables carry a `source` field naming their
prov
enance and the kaomoji generator names its own; no era field was invented for them, because a field
added only to hold a note is a field that will drift.
### What each judge does with an exception, and how the strict one seeds itself
- Allow mode derives its seed from the assembled rules and every loaded palette face, recomputed on
each resolve. Without that it would refuse the very characters it ships - a strict judge that cannot
read its own palette is not strict, it is broken. A face added at runtime is covered on the next st

ep.
- `allowExtra` admits characters under allow mode, and withdraws them from the judgement list un

der
deny mode. In deny mode that also rewrites the list the agent reads, so an exception is stated i

n the
instruction rather than only applied in the checker.
- The judge travels with the rules rather

than being frozen at registration, so switching mode, editing
the palette or naming an exception la
nds on the next step of a session that is already running.
### Why editing that file needs no restart

The section registers `text` as a **function**. The prompt registry calls it while assembling the
pr

ompt for each model step, so whatever the files say at that moment is what the agent is given.
Edit

the config file or a library file and the next step of every running session - and every new
convers

ation - reads the new wording, with no host restart. Setting `enabled: false` likewise takes
effect

ew wording, with no host restart. Setting `enabled: false` likewise takes
effect from the next step.
The resolver stats the config file and each library file and only re-reads them when a stamp (size a

nd
mtime) changes, so a step pays a few `stat` calls and nothing more.
Two layers apply, highest last: the packaged text in `src/index.js` for the chosen locale, then your
config file. `rules/<locale>.json` is **not** a third layer - see below. A config file that is miss

ing
or malformed falls back to the packaged rules, and a malformed one is also warned about, because

a
broken rules file must never keep a host from booting.
### Seeing what the rules resolve to

## What it can and cannot do
This is a layer of **rules and self-checks**, not a hard language constraint. Being exact about the

difference
matters more than sounding capable:
- The rule text is rebuilt on every step, so a config change or a new locale takes effect on the nex

t step
without restarting the host.
- The self-check runs four judgements each step (judgement glyph

s, the kaomoji floor, emoji, thinking language)
and escalates through three tiers at ten, fifty and

two hundred.
- Three levers wait at the turn boundary - a banned glyph, a missing face, an emoji - a

nd they share one
once-per-turn ledger, so whichever fires first claims the turn and they cannot sta

ck.
- A fourth lever watches what a write puts into a file.
